turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Nice to meet you. Well, honestly, it took me a while to actually make this appointment because I kept telling myself it wasn't a big deal, but... what really made me finally come in is what's been happening at work lately. I'm an advertising sales agent, and it's a really dynamic job, which I usually love, but we have these huge, sprawling sales strategy meetings. I mean, they block out hours for these things, and we're all crammed into the main conference room going over quarterly projections and client pitches. 

And the thing is, I know I’m supposed to just stay seated and look attentive like everyone else on the team, but I just... I keep getting up. I really can't help it. It's like this physical itch I have to scratch. I'll find absolutely any excuse to leave my chair, even if it’s just to refill my water bottle for the third time in an hour, or sometimes I'll just go stand and pace by the printer in the corner like I'm waiting for a document that doesn't even exist. My coworkers are starting to give me these looks, and I just feel so unprofessional because I'm thirty years old and I should be able to sit through a strategy session without needing to wander around the room. It’s just so frustrating because I want to stay put, I really do, and I tell myself beforehand that I'm going to just sit there, but my body is just like, "nope, time to move," and then I'm out of my seat again before I even consciously decide to do it.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also have trouble paying attention or staying focused?

Oh, definitely. Yes. It's actually a huge problem, and it kind of ties into the whole meeting thing I was just talking about. Like, I’ll be in those same strategy meetings, right? And I go in with the best intentions. I’ve got my notebook out, my favorite pen, I’ve had my coffee, and I’m looking right at the presenter. I’m thinking, "Okay, we are going to nail these quarterly projections." And for the first few minutes, I’m totally locked in. I’m following the numbers, I’m nodding along. 

But then... it’s like someone just unplugs a cord in my brain. I won’t even realize it’s happening at first. I’ll just suddenly snap back to reality and realize I’ve been staring at the exact same PowerPoint slide—like, maybe a graph about Q3 ad spend—for what feels like ten minutes, and I have absolutely zero idea what the person at the front of the room just said. Nothing. It’s a complete blank. 

And it’s not just in meetings, either. It happens when I’m by myself at my desk, trying to read through a new client brief. These briefs are so important, you know? They have all the details about what the client wants for their campaign, their target demographics, their brand voice, all of that. I’ll start reading, and I’m reading the words, but after a paragraph or two, I realize I’m just moving my eyes across the page. I’m not absorbing a single thing. I’ll have to go back and re-read the same paragraph three, four, maybe five times before it actually sticks in my head. It’s exhausting, honestly. I feel like I’m working twice as hard just to keep up with the basic information everyone else seems to just absorb on the first try. It’s like my brain just decides it’s done paying attention, even when I really, really need it to.

My teachers would literally have to make me stay inside during recess sometimes just to empty the whole thing out on the floor and sort through it because things were just getting lost in the abyss. 

So, yeah, when I think about it, this isn't really a new thing at all. It's just... it's just the adult version of it now, I guess. Instead of a desk stuffed with half-finished coloring pages, it's my email inbox and my client briefs, which is why it feels so much more stressful and embarrassing now that I'm supposed to be a professional. turns.doctor_question: Do you often interrupt other people before they finish speaking?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, god, yes. All the time. It’s actually one of the things I’m most self-conscious about, especially in my line of work where communication is literally everything. Like, I’ll be in a pitch or even just a casual catch-up with a client, and they’ll start asking a question—and my brain just immediately races ahead. I’ll think I know exactly where they’re going with it, so I just... I often just jump right in with an answer before a client or a coworker has even finished asking the question. 

And it’s so embarrassing because half the time, they finish their thought while I’m talking over them, and I realize I answered the completely wrong thing, or I just totally cut them off and derailed their whole point. 

Like, just last week, my manager was trying to ask me about the timeline for a digital campaign, and she goes, "For the new social push, are we thinking—" and I just instantly blurted out, "Yes, the graphics are done!" And she just stared at me, took this long breath, and said, "...are we thinking of launching on Tuesday or Wednesday?" I just wanted the floor to swallow me whole. 

I do it with clients, too, which is obviously even worse. They’ll be asking about target demographics and I’m already spitting out pricing options before they even hit the question mark at the end of their sentence. I can see them get this slight look on their face, like, "Did she really just interrupt me?" And I know how incredibly rude it comes across! I really do. It’s not that I don’t value what they’re saying or that I'm not listening, it’s just like my mouth is moving faster than my impulse control. The words are already out there in the air before I can tell myself to just bite my tongue, take a breath, and wait my turn. It makes me seem so impatient and scattered, and I just... I hate it, but I can't seem to stop doing it no matter how much I tell myself to just wait for people to finish speaking.

Um... you know, it’s funny, because after just telling you how I blurt things out and interrupt people, you’d probably think the answer would be a huge yes. But actually... no. Not at all, really.

In my job, you know, doing advertising sales, there’s a lot of pressure to make quick calls on deals or negotiate on the fly, but I never just jump into things. I always have to take a step back, look at the client history, review the numbers... I'm very cautious about what I actually commit to.

And for bigger things? It's even worse. I drove my boyfriend completely crazy because I just would not pull the trigger and make a choice.

Because my mouth will just run off without my permission in a conversation, but if I actually have to take a physical action or make a choice, I freeze up and over-analyze every single possible outcome. turns.doctor_question: Before age 12, did you often have trouble staying seated when you were expected to remain in your seat?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, definitely. I mean, I remember all of this starting way, way before high school. It was definitely happening long before I was twelve. If you look at my elementary school report cards—my mom actually kept all of them in this big plastic storage bin in her basement, and we were looking through them a couple of Thanksgivings ago—every single teacher basically wrote the exact same thing about me year after year. 

They always said I was a really bright kid, which was nice of them, I guess, but they always followed it up by saying that I constantly rushed through everything I did. And the talking out of turn was a huge issue. I just could never raise my hand and wait, I would just blurt things out, or I'd be turning around in my seat, or just getting up entirely to go talk to the kid at the desk behind me because I couldn't bear to just sit there quietly and wait for the next thing to happen. 

And the organization... or, well, the total lack of it. My teachers were always writing notes home because I constantly forgot my homework. Half the time I actually did the homework but I would just leave it on the kitchen table, or it would get completely swallowed up by my desk at school. My desk was a total disaster zone. It was just stuffed to the absolute brim with half-finished papers, squished folders, stray markers without the caps on... just a complete mess. Whenever we had to clean our desks out on Friday afternoons, it was like an archaeological dig just to find the bottom of it. I would pull out assignments from two months prior that I had just given up on halfway through. 

My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—or wait, maybe it was Mrs. Higgins? No, Higgins was fourth grade. Anyway, she was this very strict, tidy woman, and it drove her absolutely crazy that my space was always overflowing with all these abandoned worksheets and that I couldn't just stay in my chair like the other kids. So, yeah, this whole feeling of being rushed and scattered and not being able to just sit still and do what I was supposed to do... it’s been there since I was really little. It's funny how you don't realize it's a pattern until you look back at all those old teacher comments stacked up together, you know?

turns.doctor_question: Do you also tend to fidget, tap your hands or feet, or otherwise feel like you need to move around a lot?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. Like I was just saying about the brunch with my sister, I am just constantly in motion. It's like I have this internal motor that just won't shut off, and the energy has to go somewhere. 

If I'm sitting at my desk—which I have to do a lot for my job, obviously, since I'm doing all these client calls and putting together proposals—my leg is just bouncing up and down non-stop. Like, a million miles a minute. I actually had a coworker, Dave, who sits in the desk cluster next to mine, and he actually stood up and looked over the partition once because the vibration from my foot tapping was shaking his monitors. I felt so incredibly bad, but I honestly didn't even realize I was doing it! 

And if it's not my feet, it's my hands. I am a serial pen clicker. I'll just sit there, click, click, click, click, while I'm trying to read an email. I've had people on Zoom calls actually ask me to mute myself because they could hear me playing with my pen or tapping my nails on the desk. I try to buy those pens with the twist tops now instead of the clicky ones, just to save everyone's sanity, but then I just end up twisting it back and forth until the pen falls apart in my hands. 

I just... I don't know, I just have this overwhelming urge to be doing *something* with my body. Even when I'm at home, trying to watch TV and unwind after a long day of sales pitches, I can't just sit on the couch. I have to be stretching, or getting up to check the fridge every ten minutes even though I'm not hungry, or picking at the seams on the throw pillows. It’s just this constant, restless energy. If I try to force myself to stay perfectly still, it almost physically hurts, like my muscles get all tight and my skin starts to feel like it's itching. So, yeah, the tapping and the fidgeting is definitely a constant thing for me.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes constantly bouncing their leg, tapping their foot, clicking pens, and tapping their nails.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes having a constant, restless energy and an overwhelming urge to do something with their body, feeling physical discomfort if forced to stay still.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states they are constantly in motion and feel as though they have an internal motor that won't shut off.

turns.doctor_question: Do your restlessness and need to move ever cause problems outside of work, like at home or in social settings?
turns.patient_response:
Well, outside of work, I mean... I guess it definitely annoys my sister, like I mentioned with the whole brunch situation, and my boyfriend gets pretty frustrated when we're trying to just have a quiet night in. We'll be trying to watch a movie and I'm getting up a million times to check my phone in the kitchen, or I'm shaking the entire sofa because my leg is bouncing. He always ends up just putting his hand heavily on my knee to get me to stop, which is sweet of him to not yell at me, but it definitely makes me feel a bit guilty that I can't just relax with him. 

But honestly? Where it's really, really becoming a massive issue—and this is what's actually keeping me up at night and making me so incredibly anxious lately—is at work. It has actually started showing up in my performance reviews, which is terrifying. My manager sat me down for my quarterly evaluation last month, and we had this whole long conversation because my fidgeting and constant moving around is apparently starting to affect client trust. 

Which is just... it's so devastating to hear, because I care *so* much about doing good work. I really, really do. I put my heart into building these advertising campaigns and understanding what the clients need. But there was this one specific client complaint recently... oh my gosh, it was just awful. We were in a huge, important pitch meeting, and I guess I was doing the pen clicking thing, and shifting in my chair constantly, and kind of pacing a little too frantically when it was my turn to present. And the client actually reached out to my boss afterward and said I seemed "unprofessional" and "disengaged," like I wanted to be literally anywhere else but in that room with them. 

That just completely crushed me. It made me so worried that I could actually damage these accounts that I've worked so hard to build up over the last two years. Like, I'm trying my absolute best, and I'm super invested in their success, but my body just won't cooperate and sit still, and now it's actually threatening my livelihood and how people see me professionally. It's just so frustrating when your intentions are good but your physical restlessness makes people think you don't care, you know? So, yeah, it affects things at home a bit, but the work stuff... that's the part that really has me scared right now.

turns.doctor_question: As a child, did your teachers or parents ever describe you as disruptive or causing trouble in class?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I mean... I wouldn't say "disruptive" in the sense of being a bad kid, you know? Like, I was never the one pulling fire alarms or throwing things across the room or getting sent to the principal's office for being mean to other students. I was actually a pretty happy, friendly kid. My parents always said I was just very "spirited" or "bubbly." But... I guess if you mean disruptive in terms of just not being able to blend into the background and be quiet, then yeah, probably. 

Like I was saying earlier about Mrs. Higgins—or wait, no, Mrs. Gable, the third-grade teacher, I always get those two mixed up because their classrooms were right next to each other down that long hallway with the weird green carpet. Anyway, she definitely got frustrated with me. But it wasn't because I was trying to cause trouble! It was just... I just had so much to say, and I couldn't hold it in. If she asked a question about, I don't know, the water cycle, and I knew the answer, my hand would shoot up, but my mouth would just open at the exact same time. I couldn't do the whole "wait to be called on" thing. It was like there was a direct wire from my brain to my mouth that bypassed the "pause" button entirely.

And I know I talked to my neighbors a lot. I'd lean over to whisper to the girl next to me—her name was Sarah, we were obsessed with those little gel pens that smelled like fruit—and I'd just want to show her a doodle or ask what she brought for lunch, and before I knew it, the teacher would be saying my name in that very specific, warning tone. "Are we paying attention?" You know that tone. 

So my parents definitely got notes home about me being overly chatty or needing to work on my self-control during quiet reading time, because I'd be shifting around or sighing loudly because I was bored. But they never really framed it as me being a troublemaker. It was always more like, "She's very enthusiastic, but she needs to learn when it's appropriate to share." Which, honestly, is something I still struggle with now when I'm on these big conference calls with the marketing team, trying not to interrupt when someone is taking way too long to get to their point... but yeah, as a kid, it was definitely more about being a chatterbox and just having too much energy for a tiny classroom, rather than intentionally trying to ruin the lesson for everyone else.

turns.doctor_question: Which causes you more trouble day to day: losing focus and forgetting things, or fidgeting and needing to move around?
turns.patient_response:
Oh wow, that is... that is a really tough question. Honestly, I don't think I can actually pick one over the other, because it’s like asking me to choose which kind of stress I prefer, you know? They just both kind of ruin my day in their own special ways, and it really just depends on the exact moment.

Like, on the one hand, the fidgeting and the moving around, as I just went on and on about, is literally threatening my job right now with the whole client perception thing. That one client who called me unprofessional? It still makes my stomach drop into my shoes every single time I think about it. It’s so visceral. So you'd think I'd immediately say that the physical restlessness is the absolute worst part. 

But then... the losing focus and forgetting things? That's just this constant, exhausting, everyday battle that completely drains me. Like, I'll be in the middle of drafting a really important proposal—like this one I was doing for a boutique hotel chain last week, where they wanted this huge, complicated multi-platform rollout for their summer campaign—and I'll just totally lose my train of thought halfway through a sentence. Or I'll spend two hours struggling to get an email worded perfectly, and then I'll completely forget to attach the actual pricing PDF when I finally hit send. And having to send that dreaded "oops, here's the attachment!" follow-up email makes me look just as unprofessional as the pen clicking does, right? 

So it's like, they both just feed into this giant, overlapping ball of anxiety for me. If I'm moving around too much, people think I don't care about them. If I'm losing focus and forgetting my attachments or losing my train of thought in a meeting, people think I'm incompetent or disorganized. I really, really can't say which one causes more trouble overall because they just... they gang up on me, I guess? It’s all just so tangled together in my daily life that I really don't have a clear answer for which is worse. I wish I could give you a straight answer, but yeah, I honestly couldn't tell you.

turns.doctor_question: As a child, were you often told that you had trouble paying attention in class?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. "Trouble paying attention" was basically my middle name on those report cards I was just talking about. My teachers would always say I was daydreaming or staring out the window, or that I just couldn't stay on task when it was time for independent work. Which... I mean, I probably was doing all of that, because the classroom was just so under-stimulating compared to whatever was going on in my head. 

But the funny thing—well, maybe not funny, more like incredibly frustrating—is that it never actually went away. It just kind of morphed into my adult life. Like, people think you just magically grow out of that phase when you graduate, but you don't. 

Even now, at the agency, whenever we have these longer strategy meetings—you know the ones, where someone is presenting a massive, seventy-page deck for a Q3 media buy and the room is just a little too warm—or if I have to sit down at my desk and read through a really dense client brief... I always go into it with the absolute best intentions. I'll sit up straight, I've got my notebook open, my pen is ready, and I tell myself, "Okay, I am going to absorb every single word of this." And I really do start out super focused! For the first few minutes, I am completely locked in and following along perfectly. 

But then... I don't even know how it happens, it's like a switch flips in my brain without my permission. Suddenly, I'll kind of snap back to reality and realize I've been staring at the exact same slide on the projector, or reading the exact same paragraph in the brief over and over again, and I have absolutely no earthly idea what the last point was. I'll just be looking at the words, and I know they're English, but they aren't computing at all. And then I have to do this whole internal panic where I try to use context clues from what the presenter is saying to figure out how much I missed, which just distracts me even more from what they're currently saying! It's so exhausting because I really do want to pay attention, especially when it's a big client, but my brain just drifts off into the ether no matter how hard I try to force it to stay on track. So yeah, they definitely told me that as a kid, but honestly, it's still exactly what I'm dealing with today.
